body:
This was the first assignment that properly forced me to stop hiding behind the question. How does someone experience it? Not read it. Not have me explain it. Actually get put inside it.

I made multiple materializations because I did not want to immediately lock the project into the same form as the original proposal. The one that stayed with me the most was the wall.

Somebody is making something visually while also talking through what they are doing. Not explaining after. While they are making it. The machine is listening to unfinished thought, half thoughts, changing their mind, why they put something somewhere, why they erase something, and it starts trying to make the work too. They do not really collaborate. They are supposed to fight.

Because collaboration assumes they want the same thing. The person is trying to keep the work connected to whatever they are actually trying to express. The AI is trying to understand it and make something more readable, efficient or consistent from it. That readable version might be close. And close is the problem.

If it is completely wrong I just say no. If it is obvious AI rubbish the project dies in thirty seconds. If it is close enough that I look at it and think yea, I could have made that, but I know I did not, then I actually have to decide whether keeping it means it has become part of my work.

The wall becomes mixed. Their marks. Its marks. Their corrections of its marks. It's response to their correction. At some point even trying to remove the machine is still teaching the machine because the correction says something about what the person wanted. That part interests me a lot. Disagreement still gives information.

The other materializations were different ways of forcing the same question into another interaction. I had the VR or spatial thinking map, more game-like versions, the authorship and ownership hearing and a larger physical proxy version. I do not think all of these are possible final capstones. They were ways of asking the question differently.

Some of the ideas were:
- An audience judging who a written work belongs to while both the human and machine can defend their contribution.
- A participant trying to lie or hide something while behaviour still leaks into what the system learns.
- The machine remembering the conversation better than the participant and then correcting them, creating that weird moment where maybe the machine is actually right.
- A larger physical presence that becomes increasingly capable of speaking and acting as the participant.

They all come back to something similar: who gets to say what counts as me?
